articles.title: Apple Creator Studio Updated With a Slew of AI Features, Along With a New Open JSON File Format for Keynote
articles.summary:
Apple Newsroom, with software news for Apple’s “Pro and Tell” week: 
Apple today introduced transformative updates to Apple Creator
Studio, the powerful collection of creative apps designed to
put studio-grade tools into the hands of modern creators across
Mac, iPad, and iPhone. Final Cut Pro for Mac now includes built-in
MotionVFX — an expansive collection of visual effects, plug-ins,
transitions, templates, and motion graphics tools — as well as
seamless editing in Pixelmator Pro. Apple’s curated Content Hub
now includes video assets and is available in Final Cut Pro. Music
creators using Logic Pro for Mac gain a new intelligent assistant
in beta, an enhanced Stem Splitter that now separates drums, and a
redesigned Browser that incorporates all sounds, with music
understanding and even a Splice library. Pixelmator Pro introduces
Generate Fill, which lets creators transform selected areas of an
image using natural language. Keynote, Pages, and Numbers
introduce new AI features in beta, including assistants that
understand document context and new Model Context Protocol (MCP)
support for workflow automation. They also add stock video in the
Content Hub and new premium themes and templates.
Apple Creator Studio updates will be available on the App Store
this November as a free update for existing subscribers.
That’s a lot. But this part at the end caught my eye:
Across Keynote, Pages, and Numbers, the Content Hub expands to
include Apple-curated stock video footage, giving creators dynamic
visuals to enhance presentations, reports, and spreadsheets.
Subscribers also gain access to a fresh collection of
professionally designed templates and themes. Keynote introduces
support for Keynote Interchange Format (.keyx), an open JSON-based
bundle file format designed to be readable and accessible to
external tools, developer workflows, and AI agents.
Jesse Bunch, engineering manager for productivity apps at Apple, on X and LinkedIn:
Our new in-app assistants can help you get things done in record
time. MCP allows you to bring your own agent if you want. And an
open source format for Keynote (and Python library!) so you can
create Keynote documents programmatically on any platform. Huge
day for Creator Studio today.
I don’t think the Python library for the new Keynote Interchange Format is out yet, but neither are the updates to the Creator Studio apps. Very cool news, along the same lines as the new JSON-based format for Xcode projects that Apple announced last month.
 ★

articles.title: This Week in Source Control: 28 October 2026
articles.summary:
Alongside package management, I follow new features and security fixes in source control clients and in the forges that host repositories, since a lot of what I build, like git-pkgs, reads git repositories and calls forge APIs. This Week in Package Management has been published every Saturday since May, and I kept putting git releases and forge news in its Elsewhere section.
Starting this week, I’m publishing that material as a separate roundup on Wednesdays. It covers clients like git, jj, gitoxide, Sapling, Mercurial and Git LFS, and forges like GitHub, GitLab, Forgejo, Gitea, Codeberg, sourcehut, Radicle and Tangled. Package managers resolving git dependencies and CI systems like GitHub Actions are covered in the Saturday post.
This first issue covers the fortnight since 11 October, with links from release feeds for those tools and forges, the Lobsters vcs tag, Hacker News and my boosts on Mastodon. In that fortnight Anthropic, GitHub, Entire and Enroute each published a post about rebuilding source control or git hosting for the volume of pushes and checkouts from coding agents.
Scaling
Redesigning source control at Anthropic (Anthropic Engineering) describes Scion, an in-house version control system that replaced git for the company’s monorepo in five months. Merges went from around 2,500 a day in May to over 30,000 a day in September. The main branch history is almost 100 GB, and CI performs around 25 million checkouts a day. Scion is designed for clients that are always online. The server stores changesets in a write-ahead log on Spanner and runs blame, history and merge queries server-side, and clients fetch only the trees and blobs they request through regional caches. Anthropic reports the new infrastructure uses 200x less CPU and memory than the git mirror fleet it replaced. In notes on the post, Simon Willison compares it to centralised systems like Subversion.
Anthropic’s Scion is heavily inspired by Mononoke (sunshowers) points out that Scion’s “derived data” for fast blame and history queries matches the design of Mononoke, the server side of Meta’s Sapling. The original post credited Sapling only for “hard-won lessons”. A follow-up compares Scion’s changesets with Mononoke’s Bonsai changesets. Anthropic has since updated its post with more detail on the projects Scion is based on.
The bridge to agent-scale Git infrastructure (Eleanor White and Victoria Dye, GitHub Blog) covers the move of GitHub’s repositories to Azure. Most repositories have two of their five replicas there, and Azure serves about half of Git traffic. Moving the busiest repositories was blocked by a repository-wide lock that every write held across a 25ms cross-region round trip. Spokes is switching to per-reference serialisation, so only writes to the same ref wait for each other, which gave 3-4x write throughput in internal tests. Object storage then joins the write quorum as a “virtual replica”, so read replicas can be stateless.
Entire, a new git forge from a company co-founded by former GitHub CEO Thomas Dohmke, is built for repositories where coding agents and people push to the same branches. Its git server replicates each repository across regions, and the company’s forgemark benchmark reports pushes up to 89x faster than GitHub and 6x faster than Cursor Origin. Review happens through Trails, which run configured checks and agent-run evaluations in Daytona or E2B sandboxes on every push instead of a pull request diff. Agent sessions and prompts are synced into the repository and indexed for later agents to search.
Everyone is doing Git on S3 wrong (Enroute) looks at the write-ahead log designs for git on object storage that followed Cursor’s Continuity. Those designs send every push to a repository through one primary, and every replica keeps a full copy of the repository on disk. Enroute keeps each repository’s refs and a list of immutable object layers in a Raft-replicated log. Packfiles are rewritten on ingestion so a read from object storage needs only a few requests, and Enroute reports more than 7,600 pushes per second into a single repository. Against stock git serving a repacked linux.git, full clones are about 17% slower and shallow clones more than twice as fast.
Releases
GitLab 19.5 makes the GitLab MCP server and GitLab Secrets Manager, built on OpenBao, generally available. Smaller changes include a commit count variable for commit message templates, and commits signed by revoked GPG identities now show as unverified.
Forgejo 17.0 resolves absolute links in rendered documents against the repository root, as other forges do, and deprecates action run webhook events in favour of workflow run events. It also adds a Donate button driven by FUNDING.yml, migration from Bitbucket Data Center, and opt-in invitations for organisation membership. Forgejo 17.0.1, 16.0.7 and 15.0.11 followed on 26 October as security releases. The main fix stops a pull_request_review event running an Actions workflow as trusted from an arbitrary commit, including one from a fork, by ignoring the unvalidated commit_id on the submitted review. 17.0.1 also carries bug fixes for 17.0.0, which the project had advised holding off from after reports of blocked pushes and merges.
GitRoot 0.5.0, a self-hosted forge with no database that is extended through WASM plugins, now references plugins by PURL with a checksum qualifier in place of separate URL, checksum and version fields. New per-forge and per-repository settings cap how many branches anonymous users can push before further anonymous pushes are rejected.
Pushin.eu, an invite-only forge hosted in the EU, shipped several releases this fortnight according to its changelog. 0.3.26 adds tag-based releases with a GitHub-compatible API and GoReleaser publishing, and 0.3.29 serves public repository files from raw.pushin.eu. 0.3.32 adds runner groups for self-hosted runners and removes the per-repository allow_persistent_runners setting.
forges (Daniel Roe) is a TypeScript version of my Go library git-pkgs/forge, with one interface for issues, pull requests, notifications, checks and webhooks across GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket, Forgejo, Gitea, Gitee, Azure DevOps, Cursor Origin, Tangled, Pushin.eu and Sourcehut. Each provider declares which operations it supports, and the release notes show the capability changes per forge. 0.1.0 came out on 11 October, and 0.3.0 adds branch rules and review threads.
gt 0.1.0 replaces tea, Gitea’s command line tool, with a rewrite under a new name and repository. Every list and view command supports --json and --jq, and gt pr checkout and gt pr diff handle fork and AGit pull requests. It requires Gitea 28 or newer.
gitoxide 0.61.0 moves the plumbing crates to a standard std::error::Error compatible error type and improves tracing across commands, along with security fixes.
Security
Git LFS 3.8.1 fixes four CVEs:
unquoted arguments in remote commands sent over SSH
Cookie headers forwarded to other hosts after a redirect
an arbitrary program run from a malicious repository through line feeds in a submodule URL
an arbitrary program run from a malicious repository through a custom transfer adapter set in .lfsconfig
GitLab shipped two critical patch releases for integer overflows in its regular expression compiler that allowed unauthenticated code execution. The first, on 12 October, fixed CVE-2026-97229 in CI configuration patterns, and a 21 October release fixed CVE-2026-110264, which affects every version from 7.0 and was backported as far as 18.11.13. The underlying bugs are in Ruby’s Onigmo, whose fixes were in last week’s package management roundup.
Gitea 28.2.0 discloses 13 CVEs, two of them fixed in earlier releases. One fix limits which stored public keys an SSH certificate principal is matched against. Before the fix, matching against every stored key let a certificate authenticate as a different user.
git-annex 10.20261026 fixes CVE-2026-112818, a cross-repository exfiltration attack found by Joey Hess. A repository the victim clones can autoenable a special remote that points at the victim’s own private git-annex storage, so a later git-annex sync --content reads the private files and sends them to the attacker. After the fix, enableremote requires the special remote’s configuration to be verified, and git-annex refuses to send content to an unverified autoenabled remote.
Gheist (Rami McCarthy and Hila Ramati, Wiz) is a campaign that used stolen GitHub tokens to push a workflow to every reachable repository. The workflow writes repository secrets to its log in base32 so GitHub’s masking leaves them unredacted, and the attacker’s tool fetches the log over the API and deletes the run seconds later. GitHub’s hold on potentially malicious workflows in public repositories, in place since 28 July, blocked the payload there. Private repositories and GitHub Enterprise Server fall outside that hold, and Wiz observed successful runs and follow-on AWS activity from those.
An attacker took over a developer’s GitHub account and replaced OVHcloud CLI releases 0.11.0 to 0.15.0 with builds that read secrets from disk. Release immutability was turned off on the repository, so the attacker could overwrite the existing releases directly and skip CI.
GitHub
Push attribution, in limited preview for Enterprise customers, records the authenticated user who pushed each commit alongside the author and committer fields. A new “Committer must match pusher” ruleset condition accepts a push only when the committer matches one of the pusher’s verified email addresses.
During periods of unusual traffic, unauthenticated HTTPS clones and fetches of public repositories may require authentication, while SSH, authenticated HTTPS and pushes work as before.
GitHub CLI 2.103.0 adds gh auth login --expiring for refreshable tokens that expire within hours. Used as a git credential helper, it requires git 2.46 or newer, which discards a cached credential when it expires.
Repositories can now convert all their branch protection rules to rulesets in one step, with a preview before anything changes. A new repository_creation:write permission lets apps and fine-grained tokens create repositories with only that permission instead of full repository administration.
On the Files changed tab of a pull request, the whitespace visibility setting can be saved so it applies across pull requests, and new and deleted files now span both columns in split view.
Email notifications for push events have been retired because recipients could be added without consenting.
Elsewhere
Haxy, now in preview, is a local-first forge written in Zig that stores issues, pull requests and discussions as events on a haxy/events branch and serves a TUI over SSH alongside its web interface.
Making git hooks visible in fish shell (Chris R) ports Ned Batchelder’s zsh function, which lists a repository’s executable hooks when you cd into it, after Frank Wiles nearly fell for an attack hidden in a shared hooks folder.
jwz has created a GitHub repository whose only content is a README stating that XScreenSaver releases are published only as tarballs on the XScreenSaver website and that other repositories are unofficial.
Send links for next week to @andrewnez@mastodon.social.

articles.title: ★ Prestructured WYSIWYG
articles.summary:
One of the many small pleasures of my job is when someone else writes a good take on a subject that I have been meaning to write myself. Occasionally this stings, because it was something I really wanted to write myself. But usually it’s just awesome, because it’s an article I wanted to exist, didn’t really want to do the work of writing myself, and now it exists and I can just link to it, perhaps with commentary. It’s like finding money on the ground or in the pocket of a jacket you haven’t worn in months.
That’s what happened yesterday with Glenn Fleishman’s “Why Notes Will Never Let Us Edit Markdown”, and my link to it. Found money!
But one of the reasons I’d been procrastinating on writing about Apple Notes and its growing support for Markdown import/export and copy/paste is that Notes is built around a text formatting idea that, to my knowledge, doesn’t really have a name. And without a name, it’s hard to write about. I’m going to suggest calling it prestructured WYSIWYG.
Apps like Apple’s Messages and especially Notes exemplify prestructured WYSIWYG, and I’m a huge fan of the idea. It’s low-key one of the best ideas and trends in software design of the last 15 years or so. Messages lets you apply WYSIWYG spans of character styles like bold and italics, but you can’t choose typefaces or define your own styles. Notes takes this further, adding inline hyperlinks and predefined block styles like title / heading / subheading, monostyled (e.g. for code), and ordered and unordered lists. But there is no Font menu or preference setting in Notes or Messages to change the default typeface. The “Aᴀ” formatting popover in Notes doesn’t have a control to change the typeface, only its preset styles, all of which are rendered in your notes using Apple’s San Francisco system font family.1 That would have seemed not just weird but downright wrong back in the early decades of the Mac (the era Fleishman calls the “Mac Is Not a Typewriter” era, referencing Robin Williams’s groundbreaking book). In those days, text was either plain text (a string of characters, no style at all, like a typewriter) or rich text, and if it was rich text, you expected to choose any font (and size) you wanted.
That era of anything-goes WYSIWYG presented unavoidable problems. On the technical side, the list of fonts installed on my computer isn’t the same as the list of fonts on your computer. Each operating system comes with its own set of included fonts. And the sort of people most interested in selecting their own typefaces are exactly the same people who are most likely to install third-party fonts. That’s a technical problem that can’t really be solved. There’s also an aesthetic problem. Most people, given the ability to choose their own fonts, make terrible typographic choices.
Prestructured WYSIWYG solves both problems. You get the expressiveness of abstract semantic styles like bold, italics, and monospace, and you get larger sizes for headings. But you avoid both the “missing font” technical problems and the “terrible font” design choices. If you use Apple Notes or Messages, you better like Apple’s San Francisco system font family, because that’s what you’re going to get. It’s great for accessibility, because all the type sizes are relative, not absolute. And these preset styles largely map well to Markdown, which itself has no concern with font choices or specific text sizes.
Even if you’re a decent designer (or believe yourself to be), it’s liberating not to have a say in the matter in certain contexts. Note-taking is exactly such a context. Email ought to be another, but alas, full-fledged WYSIWYG gained a foothold there long ago, and now it’s entrenched. Constraints are sometimes freeing.
There is a huge but here. Notes, on the Mac and only on the Mac, does allow you to pick arbitrary fonts. Format → Font → Show Fonts (⌘T) shows the standard AppKit Fonts palette, and you can use that to change the font in a note to anything you want. I think this is historical baggage from earlier versions of the Notes app for Mac. Or maybe there are some Mac Notes users inside Apple who really do use this. Font choices made in Notes on the Mac are rendered on iOS and iPadOS, if the selected font is available. It even works for third-party fonts (which are quite complicated to install on iOS). Here’s a screenshot of a note with custom fonts that I made on my Mac, and the same note as it appears on iOS, where only some of those fonts are installed. But you cannot change custom fonts in Notes on iOS.
I can’t say Apple discourages you from dicking around with fonts in Notes on the Mac. It’s right there in the standard AppKit Fonts panel. But most casual Mac users don’t know about the standard AppKit Fonts panel. When they pick fonts in apps like Mail, TextEdit, and Pages, they do it from toolbars in the window. So Apple doesn’t encourage you to dick around with fonts in Notes on the Mac either. If they wanted to encourage it, there’d be a toolbar with a Font menu on the Mac, and it would be possible to change fonts on iOS too.
So I say it’s best to pretend that Apple Notes doesn’t support custom font choices. Let it go — even if, like me, it drives you crazy that Notes and only Notes uses that childish-looking alternative single-story “a” glyph in San Francisco. ↩︎
articles.comment: 提出了“prestructured WYSIWYG”这一原创概念，深入剖析了Apple Notes的独特文本编辑哲学。
articles.reason: 其对文本编辑设计模式的独到见解和命名，对产品设计师和UI/UX专家具有启发意义。

articles.title: Guessing the Name: MacBook Studio?
articles.summary:
Joe Rossignol, MacRumors:
A teaser video shared by Apple CEO John Ternus today hints at
a potential name for the rumored MacBook models with touch-enabled
OLED displays: MacBook Studio. [...]
Apple is expected to show off the new MacBooks to selected tech
reporters and content creators at an experience in Los Angeles at
10 a.m. Pacific Time today, and that is the home of Hollywood
movie studios after all.
I went to bed last night thinking “MacBook Studio” was the best guess. I woke up this morning feeling like it was a name worth betting on. It just fits. There’s a Mac Studio desktop, Studio Display monitor, and Apple’s suite of pro software tools is named Creator Studio — and they just announced big updates to that yesterday. As I suggested yesterday, these should be a new MacBook line, not the new MacBook Pros.
If this is the name, Rossignol gets the Being Right Point for calling it.
(A bunch of readers chimed in to suggest “MacBook Touch”. That wouldn’t work for the same reasons that Apple didn’t even consider calling the Duo the “iPhone Fold”. Yes, they used “Touch” for the iPod Touch of yore, but (a) that was a different era, and (b) that was such a mediocre product name that most consumers referred to it by the wrong name, “iTouch”. Apple likes names that evoke a feeling, not that describe a specific feature of the product.)
Update: Welp, never mind.
 ★
articles.comment: 一篇基于Apple现有产品线对新MacBook名称进行的有趣猜想，娱乐性大于实用性。
articles.reason: 及时捕捉Apple新品发布前的市场热点，能够引发社群讨论和关注。

articles.title: Pluralistic: Agents vs ecommerce (28 Oct 2026)
articles.summary: Today's links Agents vs ecommerce: Opacity is a feature, not a bug. Hey look at this: Delights to delectate. Object permanence: Aibo hacking; Calculator watches; What hath Occupy wrought; Dr Seuss v Trek parody; "Blacks for Trump" x murder-cults; "9 Times My Work Has Been Ripped Off." Upcoming appearances: Vienna, Kilkenny, Courtenay, Vancouver, Folkestone, Oxford, Sheffield, Virtual, Oxford, Montreal. Recent appearances: Where I've been. Latest books: You keep readin' em, I'll keep writin' 'em. Upcoming books: Like I said, I'll keep writin' 'em. Colophon: All the rest. Agents vs ecommerce (permalink) The first widely read piece of tech criticism I ever wrote was "Metacrap: Putting the torch to the seven strawmen of the meta-utopia," a response to the underlying philosophy of the "Semantic Web" that I published in 2001: https://people.well.com/user/doctorow/metacrap.htm The piece holds up surprisingly well today (if I do say so myself), and not just for its criticism of the ontological incoherence of "web semantics." The most relevant concept I develop in that piece is a criticism of any plan that starts with "first, everyone else in the world just needs to set aside their needs and advantages in favor of my priorities, and then my plan will work." This is especially relevant today in the context of "agentic AI." When this idea was first mooted, the big idea was that you could instruct a chatbot to venture out onto the public, unstructured web and it would do your bidding, for example, finding all the flights that fit your criteria and comparing prices for all of them, picking the best one and booking it for you. This idea quickly foundered. Each step in that process was too complex and specialized for a single chatbot; so the notion quickly gave way to "swarms" of specialized chatbots – one to search the web and identify likely travel websites; one to search those websites; one to evaluate flights against your criteria, one to handle the transaction, and so on. Through specialization, these bots could be made far more accurate, but at a price: both the literal price of all the extra computation that goes into powering a "swarm" versus a single process, and the reliability price that arises from complexity. That's because error rates are multiplicative: combine two bots with low failure rates into a single system and that system will have a higher failure rate than any of its components. This compounding error rate only increases as you add more and more bots, so every time you add a new specialized bot to decrease the error rate in its area of specialization, you increase the overall error rate of the system by adding more complexity to it. Despite this, companies pressed on ahead with "agentic," without any regard to the realities or consequences. For example, Microsoft has repeatedly announced that it will modify Windows to eliminate all forms of PC-side privacy and confidentiality, sending a continuous stream of screenshots to Microsoft's cloud servers so that your Microsoft "agent" can access your private data on Microsoft's cloud: https://pluralistic.net/2026/01/06/1000x-liability/#graceful-failure-modes But the real fix for "agentic" is for everyone in the world to rearrange their affairs to the benefit of AI agents. This is the same demand that the Semantic Web people made in the early oughts, and it has the same problems. The Semantic Web people operated on the assumption that there were freestanding, objectively correct ways of describing things and that everyone who put information on the web would eventually come to see that adopting these correct semantics was to everyone's advantage. In reality, these semantic differences are the expression of real, serious, unresolvable philosophical, technical, moral and political arguments. The reason that some media outlets won't describe transwomen as women isn't because they lack an appreciation of objectively correct semantic classifications – it's because they're bigots. That's the same reason "race realists" insist that there is a biological category called "race," that exists despite everything computational genomics has proved: https://pluralistic.net/2020/08/16/combat-wheelchairs/#race-realism In my book The Reverse Centaur's Guide to Life After AI, I predicted that a similar dynamic would play out when it came to agentic AI and websites. The reason websites are so inhospitable to bots is that ecommerce sites don't want to be legible to automated tools: https://us.macmillan.com/books/9780374621568/thereversecentaursguidetolifeafterai/ Ecommerce websites deploy a wide range of sleazy tactics to raise prices, including surveillance pricing: https://pluralistic.net/2026/10/07/gouged/#aeropain They use market power to rig whole categories, forcing prices up: https://pluralistic.net/2026/10/15/enshittipedia/ Multiple law-enforcers, Republic and Democrat, state and federal, have sued companies for "drip pricing" and "junk fees" that make it impossible to know what the actual price is until you've spent a long-ass time going through the purchase process: https://pluralistic.net/2024/06/07/drip-drip-drip/#drip-off Surveillance pricing, drip pricing, junk fees, price fixing and "most favored nation" deals are the source of all the growth in profitability by the economy's largest, most important firms. These tactics require opacity and are antithetical to the kinds of automated comparison-shopping that agentic peddlers promise: https://pluralistic.net/2024/08/14/the-price-is-wright/#enforcement-priorities These tactics are facially illegal and despite this, they are widely practiced. Cheating is so profitable that it's cheaper for firms to buy off regulators and pay fines than it is for them to stop criming. The fantasy that these same companies would welcome agentic shopping bots with open arms is just as implausible as the idea that if we feed enough words to the word-guessing program, it will wake up and become a "super intelligence": https://pluralistic.net/2026/09/18/surprise/#wow-signal What's more, the AI companies know this. Google's big plan to make AI profitable is to sell merchants the power to combine its surveillance data with its AI tools to price-gouge shoppers: https://pluralistic.net/2026/01/21/cod-marxism/#wannamaker-slain And right on time, ecommerce websites are mass-blocking AI agents: https://gizmodo.com/online-shopping-platforms-turn-against-third-party-ai-agents-2000831298 They're doing it in part because AI agents allow shoppers to cheat (for example, by renewing a "temporary" hold on a used item to block other buyers indefinitely), but also because they don't want automation tools on their platforms at all. These tools are a frontal assault on all the most exciting (and sleaziest) ways to make money in the waning hours of end-stage capitalism. Far from welcoming bots, ecommerce sites were always going to block them. It's easy to come up with amazing applications for technology if you're allowed to assume that you can get everyone else in the world to set aside their priorities and their interests in favor of yours. But unless someone has a plan to do that, we shouldn't take them seriously. articles.title: Psychometrics, vaccines, meat, Kowloon, luggage destruction
articles.summary:
This is a real paper that actually exists
Assessing the Psychometric Properties of the Dynomight™ MBTI: A Comparative Analysis with the Original Myers-Briggs Type Indicator.
Journal of Psychology and Behavior Studies, 4(1), 27-37.
Zrari, A., & Sakale, S. (2024).
A cohort of n=77 participants consented to engage in the study, meeting the inclusion criteria of being currently enrolled at the Tulua institution and expressing willingness to participate in both the initial assessment and the follow-up session. To assess the longitudinal consistency of the Dynomight™ MBTI, a second administration of the test was scheduled six weeks after the initial session.
[…]
Empirical findings, as delineated in Table 1, manifested significant positive correlations across all dichotomies, indicative of a substantial concordance between the two assessments. The correlation coefficient for the Introversion-Extroversion axis was notably high (r = .938, p < .01), suggesting a pronounced alignment in the measurement of this dimension. Comparable strong correlations were observed for the Sensing-Intuition (r = .879, p < .01), Feeling-Thinking (r = .862, p < .01), and Judging-Perceiving (r = .847, p < .01) axes, underscoring the Dynomight™ MBTI’s proficiency in mirroring the evaluative scope of the original MBTI across the core personality dimensions.
“Dynomight™” is repeated in text 77 times.
Yeast vaccines
More is Different has a post on yeast-based vaccines, describing both why yeast-based vaccines are cool (if not self-evident) and how IRB rules can violate free speech and bodily autonomy make self-experimentation difficult:
Buck submitted an Institutional Review Board (IRB) proposal to gain permission to bring home the yeast and then use them to brew beer for his own consumption. To his surprise, an institutional bioethics committee withdrew the proposal from the submission portal before it could even be considered by the IRB. The committee argued that self-experimentation is strictly forbidden. Buck says he can find no written policies to that effect. The committee also argued that Buck could not eat the yeast strain unless it was first registered with the FDA as an Investigational New Drug.
[…]
Rather than continuing to fight the bioethics committee, Buck went to his home kitchen instead.
I applaud this, but I’m a little confused about what legal theory Buck is using. The National Cancer Institute is in Maryland, and Maryland has a state law that says that all human subjects research must have IRB approval. All, with no exceptions. Perhaps Buck does not live in Maryland, or believes this law is unenforceable and/or unconstitutional.
(Many institutions have policies that say that all human subjects research conducted by employees must have IRB approval, even if those employees do it at home in their free time. But as far as I can tell, the National Cancer Institute only requires this for research done as part of official duties.)
Not a Meat Eater FAQ
Erich Grunewald makes the case. I admire this post for its willingness to acknowledge tensions and to make real concessions.
Are you sure you’re not just falling for anthropomorphic bias? How do you know your compassion for animals isn’t a misfiring of caregiving instincts we have for infants?
I agree that anthropomorphism is a real phenomenon that can distort our intuitions on these questions. […] Sentience probably exists on a spectrum, as a result of its having evolved gradually over millions of years. Since humans appear to possess the highest degree of sentience, it makes sense that our closest evolutionary relatives would be more sentient than distant ones.
Cross-sectional illustrations of Kowloon Walled City
Kowloon Walled City “was an extremely densely populated and somewhat lawless enclave within the boundaries of Kowloon City of former British Hong Kong.” Here are some cross-sectional illustrations:

As a libertarian-curious person, I wish these kinds of experiments turned out less epic-cyberpunk and more boringly utopian. Also, the amount of frolicking in these illustrations strikes me as statistically anomolous.
Destroy luggage, save lives
YES:
One place I’d like to see this implemented is airplane evacuation. If the safety announcements included “In the event of an emergency evacuation, any carry-on luggage you bring will be confiscated and destroyed. You will also be fined.” we would have more JAL 516 (379 occupants, zero deaths) and less Aeroflot 1492 or Emirates 521.
Escapes
This thread lists some excellent escape attempts.
East Germany balloon escape:
They calculated the weight of the eight passengers and the craft itself to be around 750 kilograms (1,650 lb). Subsequent calculations determined a balloon capable of lifting this weight would need to hold 2,000 cubic metres (71,000 cu ft) of air heated to 100 °C (212 °F). The next calculation was the amount of material needed for the balloon, estimated to be 800 square metres (8,600 sq ft).
Great Papago Escape:
At least some of the escapees expected severe punishment for escaping; they were aware that 50 Allied prisoners of war had been executed after escape by their German captors in Stalag Luft III. However, the Camp Papago Park escapees were only limited to bread and water rations for as many days as they were absent from camp.
George Gamow:
Gamow later said that his first two attempts to defect with his wife were in 1932 and involved trying to kayak: first a planned 250-kilometer paddle over the Black Sea to Turkey, and another attempt from Murmansk to Norway. Poor weather foiled both attempts, but they had not been noticed by the authorities.
Stanislav Kurilov, candidate for most interesting man in the world:
After sunset on December 13, in stormy weather, Kurilov jumped overboard from the stern of the cruise ship, with a snorkeling mask and fins. Luckily, he was neither immediately noticed by the crew, or struck by the ship’s propeller. Because of the strong currents, it took him three nights and two days to reach the land.
Why are art films so good?
A common theory is that modern literature has shrunk into itself. There was a time when literature overlapped with entertainment and was a major cultural force. But nowadays, to be taken seriously as “literature”, a book is (allegedly) required to be so spare/ambiguous/fragmented that it can only appeal to a tiny slice of the population. Everything else is considered low-class “genre fiction”.
You can arguably see the same phenomena in other places. For example, in the golden era of jazz, jazz was pop music, whereas modern jazz is mostly for jazz nerds. Many would claim something similar is happening with modern architecture, in visual art, and various parts of academia.
But does this theory fit with film? To some degree, yes. I personally think American movies peaked in the 1970s, when there was a strong overlap between “art movies” and “popular movies”. Since then, there’s been a bit of a bifurcation: Anora earned 20× less than Deadpool & Wolverine. Often, Anora and D&W would be shown in completely differnt theaters. And James Patterson novels are not a bad approximation of “Deadpool and Wolverine, except it’s a book”.
Still, I have a question: Why are art movies so good? Sure, some of them suffer from a similar disease as modern literature. (Namely having almost no plot and consisting mostly of long still shots in which no one talks and nothing happens.) But all of the recent winners of the Palme d’Or that I’ve seen are both “true art” and also very entertaining.
(For calibration: Shoplifters, Parasite, Titane, Anatomy of a Fall, Anora.)
What’s the deal? Is there something different about films vs. books that led to this different outcome?
Ultra-processed food
Ultraprocessed foods and obesity: Interpreting the evidence
This is a criticism of RCTs that compare diets with ultra-processed food against those without for weight loss. They argue that the results could be explained by traditional nutritional properties like caloric density, soft/hard food texture, sodium, or saturated fat, rather by food reward/palatability or the effects of processing itself. Worth reading, though I’m not sure the degree to which the people who ran those RCTs would disagree. (What would it even mean for some effects to be caused by “processing itself”?)
Packing
Many of us are obsessed with optimal solutions for packing squares into a larger ambient square.

I agree that this reveals something about god’s mindset when creating the universe. But what about packing three-dimensional cubes into a larger ambient cube? I can find some math but not a single visualization or compendium of solutions.
